questions.question_english: A primary distinction between Measurement and Evaluation in educational contexts is:
options_english: Measurement is entirely qualitative in nature, whereas educational evaluation is strictly quantitative
Measurement quantifies characteristics; evaluation assigns value judgments.
Educational evaluation is conducted prior to classroom instruction, whereas measurement occurs afterward
There is no functional difference between the two terms as they are completely synonymous in pedagogy
questions.explanation_english: Measurement quantifies characteristics; evaluation assigns value judgments. Measurement involves assigning numerical values to student performance, such as recording raw scores on a test. Evaluation extends beyond quantitative measurement by interpreting those numerical results, applying qualitative judgments, and determining the overall worth, quality, or achievement level of student learning based on established educational standards.

questions.question_english: The "Halo Effect" is a common error in subjective evaluation (like essay grading or teacher appraisals). It refers to:
options_english: Giving all evaluated candidates average marks to systematically avoid grading controversy
Allowing an overall positive impression to bias scoring of specific traits
Deliberately awarding failing grades to top-performing students to motivate them further
Applying a rigid, standardized mathematical formula to scale and adjust raw test marks
questions.explanation_english: Allowing an overall positive impression to bias scoring of specific traits The Halo Effect is a cognitive evaluation bias where an evaluator's general positive impression of an individual influences the scoring of specific performance traits. In educational settings, this bias can cause teachers to rate a student's work overly favorably based on prior high performance or agreeable classroom behavior.
